meta.title: Infection Control and Hand Hygiene
sources: CDC Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC)

lessons.title: Hand Hygiene: The Single Most Important Infection Control Measure
lessons.lay_summary: Proper hand hygiene prevents more infections than any other single action. Nurses clean their hands before and after every patient contact. The WHO '5 Moments' tells you exactly when.

content.intro: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) affect approximately 1 in 10 hospitalised patients worldwide. Hand hygiene compliance by healthcare workers is the most effective and evidence-based intervention.

sections.title: WHO 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene
sections.body:
Moment 1: BEFORE touching a patient (entering the zone). Moment 2: BEFORE a clean/aseptic procedure (IV insertion, wound care, urinary catheterisation). Moment 3: AFTER body fluid exposure risk (handling specimens, suction, wound dressings). Moment 4: AFTER touching a patient (leaving the zone). Moment 5: AFTER touching patient surroundings (bed rails, call light, IV pole).
Moment 2 is often missed: hand hygiene must occur between caring for the same patient's dirty and clean sites.

sections.title: Method: ABHR vs. Soap and Water
sections.body:
Alcohol-Based Hand Rub (ABHR): 20–30 seconds, covers entire hand surface. Preferred for routine care. Works against most pathogens. Does NOT work against: Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), Norovirus spores.
Soap and Water: 40–60 seconds, mechanical removal of soil. Required for: visibly soiled hands, C. diff patients, Norovirus outbreak, before eating.
Technique matters: cover all surfaces including backs of hands, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips, wrists.

sections.title: Barriers to Hand Hygiene Compliance
sections.body: Workload and time pressure are the most cited barriers. Other barriers: skin irritation, inaccessible hand hygiene product, disagreement about guidelines, forgetfulness. Nurse-specific: gloves are NOT a substitute for hand hygiene. Gloves must be changed between patients and between dirty and clean tasks on the same patient. Artificial nails and long natural nails (>2 mm) are not permitted in clinical areas — they harbour pathogens under and around nails.

content.clinical_pearl: Gloves create a false sense of security. Studies show healthcare workers are LESS likely to perform hand hygiene when wearing gloves than when not. Remember: hands must be cleaned before donning and after removing gloves.
key_points: WHO 5 Moments: Before patient contact, Before aseptic procedure, After body fluid exposure, After patient contact, After touching surroundings
ABHR is standard; soap + water required for C. diff and visibly soiled hands
Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene
Artificial nails prohibited in clinical settings
Technique: 20–30 s ABHR; 40–60 s soap and water
references: WHO SAVE LIVES: Clean Your Hands campaign

content.intro: Standard Precautions apply to ALL patients at ALL times. Transmission-Based Precautions are added for specific pathogens based on their route of transmission.

sections.title: Standard Precautions (All Patients)
sections.body: Assume all body fluids (except sweat) are potentially infectious. Includes: hand hygiene, PPE appropriate to the task (gloves, gown, mask, eye protection), safe injection practices (never recap needles two-handed), safe handling of sharps, respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, environmental cleaning, safe handling of linen.

sections.title: Contact Precautions
sections.body: For pathogens spread by direct contact with skin or contaminated surfaces. Pathogens: MRSA, VRE, C. diff, wound infections, scabies. PPE: gown + gloves on entry. Private room or cohorting. Dedicated equipment (stethoscope, BP cuff). Visitors instructed on hand hygiene.

sections.title: Droplet Precautions
sections.body: For large respiratory droplets (>5 microns, fall within 1 m). Pathogens: influenza, pertussis, meningococcal disease, COVID-19 (droplet + airborne). PPE: surgical mask on entry (within 1 m of patient). Patient wears mask during transport.

sections.title: Airborne Precautions
sections.body: For pathogens carried on small particles (≤5 microns, can remain suspended and travel >1 m). Pathogens: TB (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), measles (rubeola), varicella-zoster (chickenpox), COVID-19 (aerosol-generating procedures). PPE: N95 respirator (fit-tested), negative-pressure room (AIIR — Airborne Infection Isolation Room). Patient transport: patient wears surgical mask; minimise transport.

content.clinical_pearl: C. diff (Clostridioides difficile) is a special case: Contact Precautions required AND alcohol hand rubs are NOT effective against spores — must use soap and water. C. diff colitis presents with watery diarrhoea, often after antibiotic use. Early isolation and thorough environmental cleaning with sporicidal agents are essential.
key_points: Standard Precautions apply to ALL patients at ALL times
Contact: MRSA, VRE, C. diff → gown + gloves on entry
Droplet: influenza, pertussis → surgical mask within 1 m
Airborne: TB, measles, varicella → N95 + negative-pressure room
C. diff requires soap and water for hand hygiene — ABHR insufficient against spores

lessons.title: Surgical Asepsis and Sterile Technique
lessons.lay_summary: Surgical asepsis means zero micro-organisms on sterile fields and instruments. Any break in technique — however brief — requires starting over.

content.intro: Surgical asepsis (sterile technique) eliminates all micro-organisms from items and areas. It differs from medical asepsis (clean technique), which reduces micro-organism numbers. Surgical asepsis is required for: invasive procedures (central line insertion, lumbar puncture, chest drain, joint aspiration, wound closure), sterile wound dressing, urinary catheterisation, surgical environments. Maintaining sterile fields requires constant vigilance — most breaks occur from inattention, not ignorance.

sections.title: Principles of Surgical Asepsis
sections.body: 1. Only sterile items contact sterile items. 2. Sterile field is monitored continuously — never leave unattended. 3. Items below the level of the sterile field are considered contaminated (table surface is the border — anything hanging below is non-sterile). 4. Sterile persons do not reach across non-sterile areas. 5. Edges of sterile packaging and containers (1-inch border) are considered non-sterile. 6. Any item of questionable sterility is considered non-sterile ('when in doubt, throw it out'). 7. Airborne contamination: minimise talking, coughing, sneezing over sterile field; face away from field when speaking if necessary; minimise personnel movement near the field.

sections.title: Surgical Hand Scrub vs ABHR
sections.body: WHO 2009 recommends: for invasive procedures with sterile gloves, surgical hand antisepsis is required (either traditional aqueous scrub or alcohol-based surgical hand rub [ABHR]). Traditional scrub: 2-5 minutes with chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine scrub brush, fingers to elbows; keep hands above elbows ('scrub up'). ABHR surgical rub: apply per manufacturer instructions (typically 3-5 min of rubbing until dry), no water; shown to be equivalent or superior for SSI prevention. Gloves: sterile gloves must be donned without contaminating the outside; open or closed glove technique. Perforation rate of surgical gloves: 18% after 1 hour — consider double-gloving for high-risk procedures.

sections.title: Surgical Site Infection (SSI) Prevention Bundle
sections.body: SSIs account for 20% of all HAIs. Prevention bundle (evidence-based): 1. Pre-operative: antiseptic shower (chlorhexidine) night before; hair removal (clippers, not razors — razors increase SSI rate 2×); glycaemic control (target glucose <10 mmol/L perioperatively). 2. Intraoperative: prophylactic antibiotics (within 60 min before incision — nurse verifies timing); maintain normothermia (hypothermia impairs immune function, impairs wound healing); minimise operating room traffic; aseptic technique throughout. 3. Post-operative: wound assessment at each dressing change; document wound healing (PUSH tool for pressure injuries; HEALING criteria for surgical wounds); recognise SSI signs: warmth, erythema, swelling, purulent discharge, increased pain, dehiscence, fever.

content.clinical_pearl: If you think the sterile field has been breached, it has been. The principle 'when in doubt, throw it out' is absolute. The cost of a new sterile pack is negligible compared to the cost of a surgical site infection — financially and in terms of patient harm. No one should feel pressured to continue with a contaminated field.
key_points: Items below the sterile field level are contaminated; 1-inch border of sterile packaging = non-sterile
Sterile field is never left unattended
Surgical ABHR rub is equivalent to traditional aqueous scrub for SSI prevention
SSI bundle: chlorhexidine shower, clippers not razors, antibiotics within 60 min of incision, normothermia
When in doubt about sterility — throw it out
references: WHO. Guidelines for safe surgery. WHO, 2009
CDC. Guideline for the prevention of surgical site infection. 2017
NICE. Guideline NG125: Surgical site infections. NICE, 2019

lessons.title: Healthcare-Associated Infections and Antimicrobial Stewardship
lessons.lay_summary: HAIs affect 1 in 10 hospitalised patients globally. Nurses are the first line of prevention — and responsible for recognising antimicrobial resistance.

content.intro: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) affect approximately 4 million patients annually in Europe alone and are a leading cause of preventable death. The four most common HAIs are: CAUTI (30-40%), pneumonia (15-20%), surgical site infection (15%), and central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI). Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — driven partly by inappropriate antibiotic use — is projected to cause 10 million deaths annually by 2050 (WHO, 2019).

sections.title: Multidrug-Resistant Organisms (MDROs): Key Pathogens
sections.body: MRSA (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus): contact precautions; screen high-risk patients (previous MRSA, recent hospitalisation, care home residents). Decolonisation: chlorhexidine body wash + mupirocin nasal ointment × 5 days. Treatment of infection: vancomycin, teicoplanin, linezolid. VRE (Vancomycin-resistant Enterococci): contact precautions; can survive on surfaces for days — environmental decontamination is critical. C. difficile (CDI): use contact precautions AND apron AND gloves; strict hand hygiene with SOAP AND WATER (ABHR is not effective against C. diff spores). Private room preferred. Treatment: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae and CRE (carbapenem-resistant): contact precautions; limited treatment options — carbapenem or new agents (ceftazidime-avibactam). Notify infection control team for all MDROs.

sections.title: Antimicrobial Stewardship: The Nurse's Role
sections.body: Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) = optimising antibiotic use to treat infections while minimising adverse effects and resistance development. Nurse contributions: 1. Obtain blood cultures BEFORE starting antibiotics (2 sets from 2 sites) — administration without cultures leads to uninterpretable results and untreatable bacteria. 2. Administer first antibiotic dose promptly (within 1 hour of order in sepsis). 3. Document allergy history accurately (true allergy vs intolerance — vomiting to penicillin is not an allergy; cross-reactivity penicillin-cephalosporin is <1-2%). 4. Monitor therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) levels: gentamicin and vancomycin require pre-dose trough levels. 5. Escalate if patient not responding or worsening (fever persisting >72h, new organ dysfunction). 6. Support de-escalation/IV-to-oral switch conversations.

content.clinical_pearl: Alcohol hand rub (ABHR) does NOT kill C. difficile spores. For any patient with diarrhoea, or known/suspected C. difficile, hand hygiene must use soap and water — not ABHR alone. This is one of the most commonly missed infection control actions. Educate all staff, visitors, and patients' families.
key_points: MRSA: contact precautions + chlorhexidine/mupirocin decolonisation
C. diff: SOAP AND WATER only — ABHR does not kill spores; contact precautions
Blood cultures × 2 sets × 2 sites BEFORE first antibiotic dose
First antibiotic dose in sepsis: within 1 hour of order
Gentamicin and vancomycin: monitor pre-dose trough levels
references: NICE. Guideline NG15: Antimicrobial stewardship. NICE, 2015
WHO. Global action plan on antimicrobial resistance. WHO, 2015
Loveday HP et al. epic3 national evidence-based guidelines. J Hospital Infection 2014;86(S1):S1-S70

flashcards.question: WHO 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene — list them.
flashcards.answer: 1. Before patient contact. 2. Before aseptic procedure. 3. After body fluid exposure risk. 4. After patient contact. 5. After touching patient surroundings.

flashcards.question: When MUST soap and water be used instead of ABHR?
flashcards.answer: Visibly soiled hands; C. difficile patients; Norovirus outbreak; before eating.

flashcards.question: What PPE is required for a patient with active pulmonary TB?
flashcards.answer: Fit-tested N95 respirator + airborne infection isolation room (negative pressure). Patient wears surgical mask during transport.

flashcards.question: What precaution type is required for a patient with MRSA wound infection?
flashcards.answer: Contact Precautions: gown + gloves on entry to room. Private room or cohort.

flashcards.question: Why are artificial nails prohibited in clinical areas?
flashcards.answer: They harbour pathogens (including gram-negative bacteria and fungi) under and around the nail, increasing infection transmission risk.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse finishes changing a surgical wound dressing on a patient in an isolation room for MRSA. Before exiting the room, which sequence correctly reflects hand hygiene practice?

options.A: Remove gloves, exit room, perform hand hygiene at hallway dispenser
options.B: Remove gown first, then gloves, then perform hand hygiene before touching door handle
options.C: Perform hand hygiene with gloves still on, then remove gloves and exit
options.D: Remove gloves and gown and exit — hand hygiene was completed before donning PPE

mcq_questions.explanation: Correct doffing sequence: gown first (contaminated outer layer), then gloves, then hand hygiene BEFORE touching the door handle to prevent contaminating the environment. Performing hand hygiene over gloves is not effective. Hand hygiene before donning is also required but not sufficient — must also perform after doffing.

mcq_questions.question: Select ALL patients for whom soap and water hand hygiene is specifically required (not just recommended) over ABHR.

options.A: A patient with Clostridioides difficile colitis
options.C: A patient with influenza A on droplet precautions
options.D: Nurse's hands are visibly soiled with blood
options.E: Nurse is about to have a meal in the break room
options.F: Patient with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) on contact precautions

mcq_questions.explanation: Soap and water is required for: C. diff patients (A — spores resist ABHR), visibly soiled hands (D), and before eating (E). MRSA (B), influenza (C), and VRE (F) do not specifically require soap — ABHR is effective for these pathogens.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is assigned to care for a patient with suspected open pulmonary tuberculosis. Place these actions in the correct order before entering the patient's room.

options.C: Confirm the patient is in a negative-pressure isolation room (AIIR)

mcq_questions.explanation: First confirm the room meets airborne isolation requirements (negative pressure — C). Then perform hand hygiene (B). Don the N95 respirator before entering any area where airborne pathogens may be present (A). Then add other PPE as required — gown and gloves (D).
